By river boat: 70 km a day downstream, 18 up (ORBIS), the upper rivers shut at low water. Unmarked towns (spaced as Chinese county seats were) and their minor roads are added as on the "Unmarked towns and tracks" layer. Herding polities ride (50 km a day over open country). layers.label: Trade routes

items.label: overland and river routes (width: local, regional, main)
towns, by the people they serve (four sizes)

layers.note: Rebuilt on the release-3 towns and tracks (same rule, only the unmarked towns changed). Goods priced as Diocletian's Price Edict priced them: by sea, river and road about 1 : 5 : 28 per km (upriver twice downriver); a ship's day costs as much as about 8 km of road haulage. Each town serves the people nearest it by that cost; trade between two towns grows with both their people and falls by a factor of e for every 270 road-km of cost (a gravity model), routed along the cheapest paths in each season (sea lanes shut in the storm months) and averaged over the year. Classes: segments carrying at least 5 %, 12 %, 30 % of the busiest one's traffic (land and sea separately); sea traffic is bundled into lanes. The scale is set, not fitted: hauling wheat 148 km by land cost 55 % of its value (Duncan-Jones 1982), so road haulage eats a staple's whole value at about 270 km. Tested on Earth: market access over this network did not explain which Roman towns of AD 150 were large (Hanson 2016; Spearman about 0 in the east), so towns are drawn by the people they serve, not by a predicted size, and the routes are a model of where trade would run, not a reconstruction. Vector files of every layer: data/vectors/. Catchments use the countryside’s cost of bringing goods into town. Shipments are routed in both directions with their own river and sailing costs; relative traffic is not tonnes. Smaller-to-smaller pairs outside the 300 largest markets are omitted. Population occupancy and political control are unchanged.
